title: Big-City AI Bans, Edtech and Staff Misconduct, and the Return of Sold a Story
author: Alexander Russo
summary: Alexander Russo's weekly education-journalism roundup leads with the sudden wave of school AI restrictions — New York City's about-face toward limiting AI use until high school, a parallel move in LAUSD, and spreading personal-device bans — framing 2026 as the moment school AI policy shifted from encouragement to containment. Russo threads that story together with the fallout from a $17 billion Meta settlement, enrollment declines, and school-closure pressures to paint a picture of districts simultaneously restricting technology and struggling with basic fiscal survival. The newsletter's most substantive original contribution is its 'Best Education Journalism of the Week' section, where Russo singles out three data-driven investigative pieces — from the Sahan Journal, the San Francisco Standard, and the Houston Chronicle — and explains specifically why each represents journalism other outlets are missing. His own editorial judgment (what counts as comprehensive, balanced, or revealing reporting) is what turns a list of headlines into a curated argument about what deserves attention in education coverage that week.
points: Russo frames NYC's and LAUSD's new AI restrictions as a genuine reversal of prior encouragement, positioning 2026 as an inflection point where big-city districts moved from cautious AI adoption to active containment.

His explicit editorial praise for the Sahan Journal, SF Standard, and Houston Chronicle pieces — citing data visualization, balance, and length as markers of quality — models a specific standard for what 'the best education journalism of the week' looks like, distinct from merely aggregating headlines.

By juxtaposing AI bans and a $17 billion Meta settlement against enrollment declines and school-closure plans in the same issue, the roundup implicitly argues that districts are fighting a technology battle and a fiscal-survival battle simultaneously, with each complicating the other.
quotes: The big education news of the week starts with New York City's dramatic new plan to limit school use of AI until high school — an about-face for the district which raises all sorts of interesting questions for parents, teachers, and other school districts around the nation.

The tech-related school news doesn't stop there, including LAUSD's new AI limits, mixed signals from states about teachers using AI, the continued spread of personal device bans, parent-led concerns about AI and school tech decisions, and some teachers' efforts to ensure kids are learning by going analogue. Meantime, tech companies just keep pushing.

It's hard nailing down the ripple effect of something like Minnesota's Operation Metro Surge. But the Sahan Journal's Becky Z. Dernbach and Cynthia Tu give some sense of the impact in this story that combines inquiries for school enrollment, data visualization, interviews with impacted students and families and more.

This profile from the San Francisco Standard's Ezra Wallach is an unusually balanced and in-depth (over 4,000 words!) portrait of one parent who became a power broker in San Francisco educational politics.

As the Houston Chronicle's Caroline Ghisolfi, Megan Menchaca and Claire Partain report, some improvements in Houston ISD schools came from a mirage: easy-to-pass college prep courses boosted school grades significantly without necessarily including any marked improvements in teaching.
